metrics_overview.en: This table compares how well different machine learning models predict the target value (HPR) using various metrics. Compared to other models like RF (R²=0.7756) and XGBoost (R²=0.7495), KNN performs significantly better. The lower the RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) and MSE (Mean Squared Error), the better the model, and KNN has the lowest values (RMSE=0.1132, MSE=0.01281). Therefore, KNN is the recommended model for predicting HPR. A practical caution is that while KNN performs best on this test set, its performance might vary when applied to real-world, unseen data, so continuous monitoring is necessary.

According to the data, the most influential features are ORP_Low (0.0376), ORP_Mid (0.0312), and Butyrate (0.0304). fig3_feature_analysis.en: This figure provides a comprehensive analysis of which chemical measurements are most important for predicting hydrogen production (HPR). It combines several methods—like feature ranking, feature importance, and correlation analysis—to give a complete picture. The main takeaway is that the combination of VFA, Butyrate, and Acetate are consistently identified as the most critical features, with VFA being the top predictor across multiple metrics. For practical use, while many features are correlated with HPR, focusing on a smaller, highly predictive subset, such as VFA, Butyrate, Acetate, and VSS, can lead to the best model performance, as shown by the KNN model achieving an R² score of 0.83014 with only 9 features.

fig5_model_comparison.en: This chart compares how well different predictive models estimate the Hydrogen Production Rate (HPR). The models tested include KNN, RF, XGBoost, SVM, and DT. The key metric here is R² (R-squared), which measures how much of the variation in HPR is explained by the model; a value closer to 1 is better. KNN performed the best, achieving an R² of 0.8172, significantly outperforming the next best model, RF, which scored 0.7756. This suggests that KNN is the most reliable tool for predicting HPR based on the available data. However, it is important to remember that model performance depends heavily on the specific dataset, and these results should be used with caution.

fig6ab_mse_r2_features.en: This chart, titled 'MSE and R² vs feature count,' helps us understand how adding more information (features) affects the accuracy of our predictions. The R² score measures how well our model explains the variation in the data, with higher values being better, and the MSE (Mean Squared Error) measures the average squared difference between predicted and actual values, with lower values being better. Overall, the KNN model performs best, achieving an R² of 0.81717 and an MSE of 0.012810 when using 9 features (VFA, Butyrate, Acetate, VSS, Propionate, Ethanol, COD-O, pH, and ORP_Low). This suggests that using a specific, optimized set of 9 features provides the best balance of predictive power and simplicity. A practical caution is that while adding features initially improves performance, the gains diminish, and using too many features can sometimes confuse the model and hurt accuracy.

model_comparison_table.en: This table compares how well different predictive models estimate the Hydrogen Production Rate (HPR). The models tested include KNN, RF, XGBoost, SVM, and DT. Furthermore, KNN had the lowest Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) at 0.1132, indicating the smallest average prediction error.
